questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: For me it was important to try and travel a bit further away than I usually would, somewhere where I had no safety blanket and was forced to stand on my own two feet. I also really wanted to go to a place I had never been before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was just absolutely amazing. I didn't really let myself have any expectations, so I wouldn't end up disappointed. Instead I ended up having the best time of my life. The people were so friendly and welcoming, the nature and culture is out of this world and uni was also a really good experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: They bombard you with welcome letters and information, so everything was fairly easy to figure out from the get-go. And both Uniflats (where I lived) and the people working at the uni-offices were helpful and eager to assist whereever you may need it.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: A lot of mails and letters from the university and from Uniflats. They had meetings in the beginning to give us all the information. You could also always contact somebody if you needed help.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Most international students end up living in a Uniflats apartment. Otago provides you with all the information as to how you apply for a flat.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I lived fairly close to campus, as did many of the international students that I know. Dunedin is small, so it is easy to get around, and easy to get to campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The flats are fine. You hear stories about mold and stuff like that, but mostly they are just cold and very minimalistic and not maintained that well, so they look and feel old . Bring warm close, Dunedin houses are not built for the winter, so it gets cold at night, even with heaters in the rooms.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You apply for courses on something called Evision before you arrive. After arriving you still have a few weeks to change courses if you want to. It is fairly easy and self-explanatory as soon as you get access to Evision.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There are always people you can write an email to, or they have help desks and info-days where you can talk to people about the different courses

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was lucky and got all the classes I applied for, though some of the ones I had looked at before I arrived were no longer available. I did end up changing some courses just before the deadline, which was perfectly fine.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look outside of your degree. You are free to take intro to astronomy, even if you study history, or programming, even if you study medicine. It is the perfect time to experiment. I ended up taking a music class, even though a study film and media, and it was really cool and I ended up loving it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Their systeme if built up so that 100-level classes are mostly first-year classes, 200-level is second year, and so on. So just be aware of that when you look at courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They are fairly similar, though you have a lot of smaller test and exams during the semester, something that I am personally not used to. I found it a bit stressful, but it also meant that the final exams did not count as much, which ended up being nice, as you would rather spend the last few weeks with your friends.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Film Music, New Zealand Cinema, and Media and Intercultural Communication

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: New Zealand Cinema is really cool, as you also learn alot of New Zealand history and about Maori culture in film and real life. So it is a window into the history and culture, but without only being about that.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: As it often happens, you find some friends, and you end up wanting to do a lot of fun stuff together, and everything unfortunately costs money. but it is worth it!

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries are a bit more expensive then back home. Especially vegetables, the closer that you get to winter. Coffee at cafés is really cheap, but be aware, most of them already close at 14-15, which is sometimes a bit annoying. Because NZ is a very multicultural country, you can find a wide variety of ingredients in the average supermarket, and that is often cheaper than back home.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a looooot of clubs and societies that you can join. The most popular one is the tramping club, which has a lot of trips to different beautiful places around New Zealand during the semester. But there is almost anything you could dream of. and it is an amazing way to meet new people.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go on hikes! See as much as you can. Rent a car and drive somewhere beautiful. Don't waste the fact that you are in one of the most extraordinary places in the world, because it truly is.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: GO ON TRIPS! Especially in nature! You can always see a town or a city, but the mountains, lakes, beaches, glaciers, fiords and so on are what makes New Zealand so unique, so don't miss it!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy, they are friendly, welcoming, and the culture is not much different than ours. Just be respectful of the Maori people, their language and their culture, it is very important.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I became close to my neighbour, who happens to be from Wellington, but I know that many people didn't talk a lot to kiwi students. But the best place would probably be one of the clubs or societies.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn't really find anything difficult. They are overly friendly in shops, which can be a bit draining sometimes.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Their friendliness and welcoming personalities and openness towards other cultures and religions.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1: Get out of your comfort zone, try new things. 2: Travel around New Zealand. 3: Make the most of your time there, but don't stress too much about what you haven't done, just enjoy what you are doing, you can't see it all in just one semester.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be open minded, try not having too many or too high expectations, just let it happen.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting out of my comfort zone and meeting new people and challenging myself academically and socially

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I was really afraid of being lonely, so far away from everything and everyone I know. But what I quickly realised is that just about everyone will feel like that when they arrive. So do not worry, you will meet tons of amazing people, and you will have the time of your life!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
